From 3: F
Since F is true and F XOR P is true, then P must be false. So: not P

Previously in 8: (T XOR S) -> M
We know not S. So (T XOR S) simplifies to T (because T XOR False is T). So the statement becomes T -> M.
From 4: not M
If T -> M and not M, then by contrapositive, not T must be true. So: not T

We have not T and not P. This means (T or P) is false.
Since I -> (T or P) and (T or P) is false, then by modus tollens, I must be false. So: not I

Consider statement 10 or 12: R or I (or not I -> R)
We have not I.
If R or I is true and I is false, then R must be true. So: R

Therefore, Kayson appreciates tradition is true.
